title: Janmashtami: the night Krishna was born
hookLine: a baby girl carried back to Kamsa's prison slips from his hands and rises as the Goddess
carry: yogamaya: no tyrant can hold god's power
last: A PRAYER OF PROTECTION, AND A PROMISE.

cards: Krishna's birth is usually told as the story of one baby: the boy carried across the flooded river. But Vasudeva didn't come back from Gokul empty-handed.

He laid his son beside the sleeping Yashoda and picked up her newborn daughter, then walked back through the storm to the prison, and the doors locked behind him. In the morning, Kamsa would come for the eighth child.
And the eighth child, now, was a girl.

teach.b: The baby cries, and the guards run to tell the king. Kamsa rushes in. Devaki begs him: you've killed my sons; this is a daughter, she can't hurt you, let me keep just this one.

In the Bhagavata's telling, he grabs the baby by the feet to dash her against a stone, and she slips out of his hands. She rises into the air, no longer a newborn: the Goddess, eight-armed, holding weapons, shining.
The text calls her Yogamaya, Vishnu's own power, who had agreed to be born to Yashoda for exactly this night. From the sky she tells Kamsa: killing me does you no good.
The one who will end you has already been born, somewhere else. Then she's gone. And the Bhagavata does something surprising.

Kamsa, shaken, apologizes to Devaki and Vasudeva and frees them from their chains. It doesn't last; by the next day his advisers have talked him back into cruelty. Here's the teaching folded into the night.

teach.h: NO TYRANT CAN HOLD GOD'S POWER.
teach.b: Kamsa has the prison, the guards, the chains and the stone, and none of it can hold God's power. That's what Yogamaya shows him.
The God who came down was born in a prison, and the darkest room in the kingdom couldn't keep him.
So on Janmashtami many families fast until midnight, then sing and rock a small cradle for baby Krishna, welcoming the one no tyrant could hold.

how: Many Hindus fast on Janmashtami until midnight, the hour of Krishna's birth, then sing, rock a small cradle with an image of baby Krishna, and break the fast; many keep the next day as Nandotsava, and in many places Yogamaya is honored as the Goddess who protected the infant Krishna.

o: Krishna's birth night, kept awake until midnight
the day Krishna was crowned king of Dvaraka
a harvest night honoring cows and cowherds

begs Kamsa to spare the girl

s: Devaki begs Kamsa to spare the baby girl
she pleads that a daughter can't hurt him; he doesn't listen.
Kamsa apologizes to Devaki and Vasudeva and frees them
the Bhagavata says he's briefly sorry, before his advisers change his mind.
the girl tells Kamsa his killer is in Gokul
she says only that the one who will end him has been born somewhere else.

games.q: a cousin asks why families wait up till midnight on Janmashtami and rock a cradle. what fits today's teaching?
o: Krishna was born at midnight in Kamsa's prison; the cradle welcomes the God no prison could hold.
midnight is when the fast is hardest, so it earns the most merit.
it's only for the kids, to make the story fun.
games.why: the God who came down was born in the darkest room in the kingdom, and Kamsa's power couldn't hold him, or Yogamaya.

practice: Many families wait up until midnight on Janmashtami. Dim the light or close your eyes, and sit in the dark a moment, the way they wait. If you pray, say Krishna's name slowly, or Hare Krishna.
If you don't, think of something that feels locked up right now, in your life or in the world. Hold it in the dark, and remember: the darkest room in the story couldn't hold what was born there.

wordCard.voice: Janmashtami. Krishna's birth night, when a boy was carried to safety and a girl carried back, who rose as Yogamaya and could not be held.

orig.note: Sanskrit yogamāyā: Vishnu's own power, born as Yashoda's daughter on Krishna's birth night.

carryVoice: Your line: yogamaya, no tyrant can hold god's power. Kamsa had the prison; he never had her. That's day six hundred eighty-four.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.4 (the girl slips from Kamsa's hands; Kamsa's apology)
